description: A team for the challenge "Build the Astronaut mission trainer",young/beginner level project.
summary:
Outpost Zero is a browser game where young players act as mission commander of a Moon or Mars outpost for 8 days. Each day they handle an event inspired by real missions, such as a solar flare, a dust storm or a water leak. Then they plan how to spend limited power and crew time across life support, water recycling, food, radiation shielding and crew morale. Forecast arrows show what tomorrow will look like, so every choice teaches a trade-off.
It addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning real habitat engineering decisions into a fun, easy-to-learn game for students. Every event includes a short NASA-based fact and a quiz question, and the final report explains how real missions handle the player’s weakest systems.
It matters because space careers start with curiosity. Kids learn that a base is an engineered system where resources compete, and that failing is a chance to learn and try again.
details:
What it does: Outpost Zero is a strategy game for kids. Players pick the Moon (Shackleton Crater rim, with a 3-day lunar night) or Mars (Jezero Crater, with dust storms and slow radio delays), and a Cadet or Commander level. Each day starts with an event such as a solar flare, a micro-meteoroid leak, a dust storm or a homesick crew. Players choose a response, and each option shows its costs first. Then they plan the day. They spend power blocks on life support, a water recycler, greenhouse lights and heaters, and assign 4 crew shifts to jobs like mining ice, building a radiation wall, tuning solar panels or resting. Six live meters (power, oxygen, water, food, shield and crew) show forecast arrows for tomorrow.

Benefits and impact: Players learn that habitats are engineered systems where resources compete. A brownout, a cold night or a missed repair has a visible effect. After every event, a real NASA fact and a quiz question reinforce the idea. The end screen has an Engineer’s Report on the two weakest systems and how real missions handle them. Failing never harms the crew, who return to Earth safely, so kids can try again.

Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG graphics and the Web Audio API, with no frameworks. It is hosted on GitHub Pages and works on phones and computers with no install. We used an AI assistant (Claude) to help write the code and text. We tested the balance by running thousands of simulated games, and tested the interface in a real browser at phone and desktop sizes.

Creativity and design choices: The forecast arrows show consequences before a choice is final. Game systems follow real mission problems like the lunar night, Martian dust storms, radiation shelters and communication delays. We made the facts short and the numbers simple for ages 8 to 14. Each game day stands for several real days. The game has a mute button, buttons that work with a keyboard, and reduced-motion support.
